item.title: Teleoperator-Aware and CBF-Based Adaptive Nonlinear MPC for Shared Autonomy in Obstacle Avoidance of Legged Robots
item.description: arXiv:2509.22815v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Safe and effective collaboration between humans and autonomous legged robots is a fundamental challenge in shared autonomy, particularly for teleoperated systems navigating cluttered environments. Shared autonomy for legged robots remains challenging due to uncertain human commands, collision-avoidance requirements, and the need to coordinate high-level planning with dynamically feasible locomotion. This paper presents a teleoperator-aware, control barrier function (CBF)-based, adaptive nonlinear model predictive control (ANMPC) framework for shared autonomy of quadrupedal robots in obstacle-avoidance tasks. The framework employs a prescribed arbitration weight between human and robot actions while modeling human inputs using a noisily rational Boltzmann model, whose parameters are adapted online through a projected gradient descent (PGD) law based on observed joystick commands. CBF constraints are incorporated into a computationally efficient NMPC formulation to promote obstacle avoidance while accounting for predicted human actions. The hierarchical architecture integrates high-level CBF-based ANMPC (10 Hz), mid-level dynamics-aware NMPC (60 Hz) enforcing single rigid body (SRB) dynamics, and low-level nonlinear whole-body control (500 Hz). Human-in-the-loop hardware experiments with ten participants on a Unitree Go2 quadruped demonstrate real-time feasibility and collision-free navigation across 50 trials. Shared autonomy reduced average human control effort by 51% and joystick activity from 88% to 42% of trial time, with comparable obstacle clearance and significantly higher perceived assistance than manual operation. Simulation-based ablation studies demonstrate improved obstacle clearance across operator rationality levels and up to a 66% reduction in median human-action prediction error through online adaptation.

item.title: Average-reward reinforcement learning in semi-Markov decision processes via relative value iteration
item.description: arXiv:2512.06218v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper applies the authors' recent results on asynchronous stochastic approximation (SA) in the Borkar-Meyn framework to reinforcement learning in average-reward semi-Markov decision processes (SMDPs). We establish the convergence of an asynchronous SA analogue of Schweitzer's classical relative value iteration algorithm, RVI Q-learning, for finite-space, weakly communicating SMDPs. In particular, we show that the algorithm converges almost surely to a compact, connected subset of solutions to the average-reward optimality equation, with convergence to a unique, sample path-dependent solution under additional stepsize and asynchrony conditions. Moreover, to make full use of the SA framework, we introduce new monotonicity conditions for estimating the optimal reward rate in RVI Q-learning. These conditions substantially expand the previously considered algorithmic framework and are addressed through novel arguments in the stability and convergence analysis of RVI Q-learning.
item.dc:creator: Huizhen Yu, Yi Wan, Richard S. Sutton

item.title: Contextual Distributionally Robust Optimization with Causal and Continuous Structure
item.description: arXiv:2601.11016v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: WWe propose a framework for contextual distributionally robust optimization (DRO) that considers the causal and continuous structure of the underlying distribution, and we develop interpretable and tractable decision rules. We first introduce the causal Sinkhorn discrepancy (CSD), an entropy-regularized causal Wasserstein distance that encourages continuous transport plans while preserving causal consistency. We then formulate a contextual DRO model with a CSD-based ambiguity set, termed Causal Sinkhorn DRO (Causal-SDRO), and derive its strong dual reformulation, where the worst-case distribution is characterized as a mixture of Gibbs distributions. To obtain an (infinite-dimensional) optimal policy, we propose a soft regression forest (SRF) decision rule: it preserves the interpretability of classical decision trees while being fully parametric, differentiable, and Lipschitz-smooth, enabling intrinsic interpretation from both global and local perspectives. To solve Causal-SDRO with parametric decision rules, we develop an efficient stochastic compositional gradient algorithm that converges to an $\varepsilon$-stationary point with $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-4})$ iteration complexity and $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-5})$ sample complexity. Finally, numerical results on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the superior performance and interpretability of our method.
item.dc:creator: Fenglin Zhang, Jie Wang

item.title: From Inexact Gradients to Byzantine Robustness: Acceleration and Optimization under Similarity
item.description: arXiv:2602.03329v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Distributed learning algorithms are vulnerable to adversarial nodes, a.k.a. Byzantine failures. To solve this issue, robust algorithms have been developed, which typically replace parameter averaging with robust aggregations. While generic conditions on these aggregations exist to guarantee the convergence of (Stochastic) Gradient Descent (SGD), the analyses remain rather ad hoc. This hinders the development of more complex robust algorithms, such as accelerated ones. In this work, we show that Byzantine-robust distributed optimization can, under standard generic assumptions, be cast as a general optimization with inexact gradient oracles, an active field of research. This allows us to obtain state-of-the-art results for Byzantine-robust optimization from general inexact first-order analyses. We first show that inexact GD on top of standard robust aggregation procedures obtains optimal asymptotic error in the Byzantine setting. Going further, we study an algorithm for Optimization under Similarity, in which the server leverages an auxiliary loss function that approximates the global loss. Then, we introduce an Accelerated Extra-gradient method that yields acceleration in both the standard and similarity settings. We first give new general convergence results for these inexact schemes, improving the tolerance level of acceleration to a relative error term by a $\kappa^{1/2}$ factor over previous analysis, and then instantiate these results in the Byzantine setting through our reduction. Both algorithms drastically reduce the communication complexity, as we show theoretically and empirically.
item.dc:creator: Renaud Gaucher, Aymeric Dieuleveut, Hadrien Hendrikx

item.title: Rare Event Analysis via Stochastic Optimal Control
item.description: arXiv:2604.13213v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Rare events, from biomolecular conformational changes and phase transitions to chemical reactions, are central to many physical systems, yet extremely difficult to study computationally because unbiased simulations seldom produce them. Transition Path Theory provides a rigorous statistical framework for analyzing such events: it characterizes the ensemble of reactive trajectories between two metastable states (reactant and product), and its central object, the committor function (the probability that the system next reaches the product rather than the reactant), encodes essential kinetic and thermodynamic information. We introduce a framework for committor estimation that builds on stochastic optimal control, with a principled formulation that grounds committor learning on capped hitting-time trajectories. In this framework the committor defines a feedback control, proportional to the gradient of its logarithm, that steers trajectories toward the reactive region, enabling sampling of reactive paths. As practical algorithms, we develop two training losses: a heuristic on-policy direct backpropagation loss and a principled off-policy Value Matching loss, for which we establish first-order optimality guarantees. Being off-policy, Value Matching can leverage simulated trajectories from alternative sampling processes and reuse them from a replay buffer, which enables efficient learning. In particular, we derive a reactive current-preserving sampling process that can accelerate exploration. On reversible and non-reversible dynamics, the framework yields more accurate committor estimates, reaction rates, and transition path samples than existing methods.
item.dc:creator: Yuanqi Du, Jiajun He, Dinghuai Zhang, Eric Vanden-Eijnden, Carles Domingo-Enrich

item.title: Characterization of stability radii for robustly asymptotically stable dissipative Hamiltonian differential-algebraic systems
item.description: arXiv:2605.13891v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study linear time-invariant dissipative Hamiltonian differential-algebraic systems. We characterize when the systems are robustly asymptotically stable and derive exact conditions and bounds when this property is lost under structure-preserving perturbations.
item.dc:creator: Peter Benner, Volker Mehrmann, Anshul Prajapati, Punit Sharma

item.title: Structured Adaptive Tensor Prediction for Streaming Data
item.description: arXiv:2606.10085v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Matrix-valued time series arise in a wide range of applications, such as spatio-temporal data in medical imaging and geophysics. Existing forecasting methods are mainly designed for static settings, while adaptive filtering techniques have been largely limited to scalar- or vector-valued data. In this paper, we develop an adaptive tensor prediction framework for streaming matrix-valued data based on a Tensor-on-Matrix (ToM) regression model, in which the responses in a sliding window are lifted to a third-order tensor and the regression tensor is updated online by stochastic gradient descent (SGD). We derive the leading terms of the steady-state and tracking errors of SGD with overlapping windows, which show that the steady-state error is proportional to the step size and the noise variance, and that the step size governs a trade-off between noise and tracking. We further analyze the statistical accuracy of structured ToM regression within a single window. We establish a restricted isometry property, which holds when the window length is proportional to the input dimension, and derive recovery error bounds for sparse, low-rank and sparse plus low-rank regression tensors, which show that the recovery error scales with the intrinsic degrees of freedom rather than the ambient dimension. Simulations confirm the theoretical results, and the effectiveness of the structured adaptive updates is validated on the tracking of a drifting quantum gate, citywide crowd-flow prediction, and global total electron content (TEC) forecasting.
item.dc:creator: Zhen Qin, Yang Chen

item.title: Convergence of Large-Stepsize SGD for the Cross-entropy Loss via Stochastic Lyapunov Stability
item.description: arXiv:2606.30930v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern deep learning has been shown to operate using learning rates far larger than those justified by classical optimization theory. Most prior analyses of this phenomenon focus on deterministic gradient descent, leaving the stochastic setting largely unexplored. In this work, we provide sharp convergence guarantees for Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) applied to the multiclass cross-entropy loss, for both linear classifiers and two-layer neural networks. We show that the stochasticity of SGD may cause the dynamics to alternate between an edge-of-stability regime that is dominated by curvature-driven oscillations, and a stable regime in which the expected loss decreases at a controlled rate. Despite that, we prove that SGD stabilizes the dynamics, ensuring that the iterates return to stability in a fixed number of iterations and allowing convergence in the best-iterate sense even with large learning rates. Experiments validate our theoretical findings and illustrate the benefits of SGD in the large-stepsize regime.
item.dc:creator: Konstantinos Emmanouilidis, Lachlan MacDonald, Salma Tarmoun, Rene Vidal

item.title: Smart predict-then-robustly-optimize
item.description: arXiv:2607.21773v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this paper, we propose and study a robust variant of the smart predict-then-optimize approach that accounts for prediction shifts due to disturbance in the covariate feature space. While traditional integrated-learning-and-optimization models assume that side information is perfectly revealed, empirical data-driven features are frequently corrupted or noisy at the time of decision-making, leading to fragile operational policies. To bridge this gap, we integrate principles of robust optimization directly into the predictive-prescriptive pipeline via a smart predict-then-robustly optimize loss and establish a computationally tractable convex surrogate, designed to hedge against worst-case feature perturbations. On the theoretical front, we formalize the structural validity of this surrogate by proving its approximation error probability decays exponentially according to a sub-Gaussian concentration profile. Furthermore, we establish that under mild assumptions, the surrogate is Fisher consistent with high probability. We also prove necessary conditions under which our framework outperforms standard smart predict-then-optimize and maintain its superiority even when the standard method is equipped with regularized upstream predictions. Numerical experiments validate that our robust framework consistently yields significant performance improvements over standard methods, both in out-of-sample terms and in training stability.
item.dc:creator: Aakil Caunhye, Xuefei Lu, Belen Martin-Barragan

item.title: A Lower Bound on the Sliced Wasserstein Comparison Constant for Translated Measures
item.description: arXiv:2607.26399v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We provide closed-form expressions for standard 1-Wasserstein distance ($W_1$) and Sliced 1-Wasserstein distance ($SW_1$) for translated probability measures on $\mathbb{R}^d$. Furthermore, we construct an explicit lower bound for the constant $c_d$ established by Carlier, Figalli, M\'erigot, and Wang between $W_1$ and $SW_1$ [1] for translated probability measures on $\mathbb{R}^d$. Sliced Wasserstein distances are computationally efficient and used in image generation and other applications, which raises natural questions in computational efficiency versus theoretical correctness. A lower bound on the constant $c_d$ gives information about the cost of that efficiency.
item.dc:creator: Avery Noroozi

item.title: The Loss Does Not See the Basis, but Adam Does
item.description: arXiv:2608.05136v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Different optimization algorithms can find very different solutions to the same problem. Gradient descent (GD) exhibits a low-rank bias in overparameterized problems when initialized near zero, while Adam does not. GD is rotationally equivariant: rotating both factors of a factored model $W = UV^\top$ by an orthogonal matrix leaves the loss unchanged, and GD's solution rotates accordingly. In contrast, Adam is not. We show that any algorithm using only the current gradient and respecting rotational symmetry amounts to a left-preconditioner depending only on the gradient's Gram matrix. This gives a norm-based test, which passes for the spectral norm in Muon and fails for Adam's $\ell_\infty$ norm. Empirically, nine optimizers fall into groups consistent with the test on underdetermined matrix sensing. Sharing Adam's second moment across coordinates gradually recovers a low-rank bias, and its solutions approach GD's as the stepsize decreases. On four hyperspectral scenes, Adam's solutions are hundreds to thousands of times further from GD's than two GD runs with different step sizes are from each other. In transformers and LoRA adapters, Adam separates two rotationally equivalent models from the first iteration, and learns higher-rank attention updates. Overall, recovering particular solutions depends on the optimizer's invisible coordinate basis, as well as how fast it grows small singular values relative to large ones.
item.dc:creator: Devender Singh

item.title: A Wasserstein Trust-Region Method for Smooth Potential-Interaction Energies
item.description: arXiv:2610.08883v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Finding low-energy particle configurations and approximating probability distributions both lead to minimizing potential-interaction energies in Wasserstein space. Second-order information can speed up minimizing these possibly nonconvex energies, but a quadratic model is accurate only near the current measure. We introduce a Wasserstein trust-region (WTR) method for smooth, possibly nonconvex energies of this type. Each iteration transports the current measure $\rho$ along a displacement field $s$, producing $(\mathrm{Id}+s)_\#\rho$. The field approximately minimizes a quadratic model built from the second variation of the energy, subject to $\|s\|_{L^2(\rho)}\le\Delta$, using a truncated conjugate-gradient method. The ratio of actual to predicted decrease determines step acceptance and updates the trust-region radius. Under a lower energy bound and globally bounded Hessians of the potential and interaction kernel, we prove that the objective is nonincreasing, the Wasserstein-gradient norms converge to zero, and an $\varepsilon$-stationary iterate is reached within $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ iterations, rejected ones included. If the potential is quadratically coercive, every weak accumulation point is stationary. For empirical measures, WTR is an ordinary trust-region method in the particle positions, and its complexity bound does not depend on the number of particles provided the initial energy exceeds its infimum by a bounded amount. For $2048$ and $4096$ particles with Gaussian pair repulsion in a two-dimensional harmonic trap, WTR reaches the gradient tolerance $2\times10^{-4}$ a median $1.40$ times faster than L-BFGS. For equal-weight integration rules on two non-Gaussian targets, WTR reaches an integration error of $10^{-4}$ about $1.8$ times faster than L-BFGS and $1.3$ times faster than a Krylov trust-region solver.
item.dc:creator: You Wan, Ting Gao, Jinqiao Duan, Jie Sun

item.title: OC-OPD: Observation-coordinated Supervision for On-Policy Distillation
item.description: arXiv:2611.01965v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reverse and forward Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergences provide complementary supervision in on-policy distillation: reverse KL refines the student's active token rankings, and forward KL allocates mass to teacher-supported candidates. At student-generated prefixes, we form a four-observation matrix by treating the student and teacher as both candidate sources and evaluators. The diagonal self-observations measure uncertainty, while source-centered cross-observations recover the two KL objectives. We establish an exact identity equating the Fisher inverse-metric coupling of their logit gradients with the sum of these contrasts, yielding a common local descent direction for distinct positive distributions. Observation-coordinated on-policy distillation (OC-OPD) uses observations to set preferences, closed-form bargaining to coordinate gradients, and distributional discrepancy to scale the update. Across three heterogeneous student settings (non-thinking generation, thinking generation, and base-model initialization), OC-OPD achieves strong gains in mathematical reasoning and transfers effectively to out-of-distribution scientific question answering and code generation. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/RuoranXu/OC-OPD.
item.dc:creator: Ruoran Xu, Yilun Zhao, Ziyu Chen, Arman Cohan

item.title: A proof of the Reinhardt conjecture
item.description: arXiv:2611.21470v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We prove the Reinhardt conjecture: among centrally symmetric convex disks in the plane, the smoothed regular octagon has the least optimal lattice packing density, and equality holds precisely for its nonsingular affine images. Local cost inequalities reduce arbitrarily long switching cycles of a minimizer to six types. We exclude those types by geometric comparisons and rigorous finite verification, and identify the remaining short minimizer.
item.dc:creator: Fei Xue

item.title: A Study of the PDE Model for the Anisotropic Consensus-Based Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.22208v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We investigate the nonlinear Fokker--Planck equation associated with anisotropic consensus-based optimization. Under suitable assumptions on the objective function, we establish global existence and uniqueness of density valued weak solutions for bounded initial probability densities with finite fourth moment. The main analytical challenge arises from the component-wise degeneracy of the diffusion, which vanishes along moving coordinate hyperplanes determined by the weighted consensus point. To overcome this difficulty, we develop spatial translation estimates based on weighted gradient bounds and uniform density estimates. Combined with temporal translation and moment estimates, these yield strong compactness in $L^2((0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^d)$ through the Fr\'echet--Kolmogorov compactness criterion, enabling passage to the limit in the regularized equations. Uniqueness is established through the associated McKean--Vlasov stochastic differential equation and Wasserstein stability of the weighted consensus point. Furthermore, we prove the propagation of $H^2$-regularity for sufficiently regular initial data.
item.dc:creator: Keyu Li, Hui Huang

item.title: Diffusion Models are Provably Efficient Priors for Sparse Recovery
item.description: arXiv:2611.24602v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Diffusion models have transformed generative modeling through their ability to capture and generate samples from complex data distributions. This success has spurred substantial interest in using pretrained diffusion models as expressive priors for highly ill-posed inverse problems in imaging and sensing. Despite strong empirical performance, theoretical understanding of this approach remains limited: existing guarantees are often asymptotic or entail prohibitive computational costs in the worst case. In this paper, we address this gap by studying sparse recovery from a small number of linear measurements, a classical problem in compressed sensing. We show that, given an accurate diffusion model capturing a sparsity-promoting Bernoulli-Gaussian prior, a likelihood-guided annealed Langevin sampler provably recovers the sparse signal in polynomial time with near-optimal sample complexity for a broad family of random and deterministic sensing matrices. When the signal is indeed drawn from the postulated prior, we further establish total variation guarantees for posterior sampling after a final denoising step. These results lay a theoretical foundation for statistically and computationally efficient inverse solvers with diffusion priors.
item.dc:creator: Ivan Lee, Xingyu Xu, Yuejie Chi
